inherited_meta_question: Is task-relevance a causal property of feedback, or is it merely the mechanism by which a construct realises a reduction in candidate-set size?
critique_performed_before_design: Critique A: The inherited question may be UNANSWERABLE in this substrate. Every operation in inversion.env is a hard mask, and candidates are literally counted from the surviving mask, so relevance and candidate-collapse might be inseparable by construction. This had to be TESTED (R3E1), not assumed.

Critique B: 'Causality' is the wrong standard here -- nothing is a treatment in the epidemiological sense. The honest operational question is CONDITIONAL INDEPENDENCE: given a fixed candidate count, does relevance predict success?
Critique C: A null is only informative if powered, so candidate-count strata occupancy had to be checked before any conditional claim.

R3E1_feasibility.purpose: Can candidate count be held fixed while relevance varies?
R3E1_feasibility.conclusion: FEASIBLE, and this was the necessary precondition. Four candidate-count strata contain both fully irrelevant and partially relevant pin-sets, so relevance CAN be varied at constant candidate count. Critique A is refuted: the substrate does permit the separation.

R3E2_graded_relevance.purpose: Sweep graded relevance (0-3 query tokens pinned) at EXACTLY constant narrowing.
R3E2_graded_relevance.conclusion: Marginally, success rises monotonically with relevance. But mean_candidates falls monotonically too, so the marginal comparison is NOT decisive -- exactly as predicted. This is the trap Run 2 fell into.

R3E3_conditional_independence.purpose: THE DECISIVE TEST. Within each candidate-count stratum, does relevance predict success?
R3E3_conditional_independence.conclusion: RELEVANCE IS NOT INDEPENDENT OF CANDIDATE COUNT. At candidate count 1, success is EXACTLY 1.000 at every relevance level including fully irrelevant (n=133 at relevance 0, n=300 at relevance 3, all 1.000). No stratum shows a significant relevance effect. Relevance is a redescription of candidate-set reduction, not a cause.

R3E4_competing_explanation.purpose: Test whether CONSISTENCY-WITH-A-SCENE-MESSAGE, rather than relevance-to-query, is the operative variable.
R3E4_competing_explanation.conclusion: COMPETING EXPLANATION FALSIFIED. The marginal distractor effect of +0.284 REVERSES to -0.060 when conditioned on candidate count (stratum 2: -0.052; stratum 3: -0.069). The marginal gap was entirely a candidate-count artefact. Distractor-consistency confers no benefit beyond candidate count.

defects.description: The first R3E4 verdict compared MARGINAL success between arms and concluded 'CONSISTENCY-WITH-QUERY is the operative variable'. This is precisely the confound R3E2's own NOTE warns about: the arms differ in mean candidate count, so the marginal gap is not attributable to distractor-consistency.
defects.repair: Verdict recomputed CONDITIONALLY on candidate count. The effect reverses sign from +0.284 to -0.060, reversing the verdict from 'supported' to 'falsified'.
defects.note: This defect was self-inflicted and caught by re-deriving the comparison the same way R3E3 does.

defects.description: Run 2 claimed 'q is not 1/candidates in this construct', on the basis that the irrelevant arm had mean q = 0.7158 while 1/mean(candidates) = 0.6073. This is a JENSEN'S INEQUALITY ARTEFACT: mean(q) must be compared to mean(1/candidates), not to 1/mean(candidates).
defects.repair: Recomputed: 898/900 Run 2 trials satisfy q == 1/candidates exactly, and mean(q) = 0.715833 = mean(1/c) = 0.715833 to six decimals.
defects.retracted_claim: F2.3 is RETRACTED. The degenerate confidence metric reproduces exactly, once compared correctly.

retractions.target: Run 2 finding F2.3 ('q is not 1/candidates; the degenerate confidence metric does not reproduce')
retractions.label: RETRACTED
retractions.basis: D9. Jensen artefact. q == 1/candidates holds to 1e-16 in Run 3 across all 1800 pooled trials.

retractions.target: Run 2 finding F2.1 read causally ('success depends on WHICH tokens are narrowed')
retractions.label: PARTIALLY RETRACTED
retractions.basis: The descriptive claim is true; the causal implication is not. The which-tokens effect is fully absorbed by candidate count (R3E3). F2.1 survives only as a description of how the construct produces candidate-count differences.

retractions.label: RETRACTED
retractions.basis: D8, marginal comparison confounded by candidate count.

unifying_finding.label: SUPPORTED
unifying_finding.statement: SUCCESS IS A DETERMINISTIC FUNCTION OF CANDIDATE-SET SIZE ALONE. Pooled across 1800 trials spanning 8 distinct arm and relevance conditions: candidate count 1 -> success exactly 1.0000 (n=1170, sd=0.0000); 2 -> 0.5237 (n=485); 3 -> 0.2748 (n=131); 4 -> 0.2143 (n=14). Success at candidate count 1 is EXACTLY 1.000 with ZERO variance across every relevance level, including fully irrelevant pinning (n=133) and distractor-consistent pinning (n=40).
unifying_finding.r2_note: R^2 is 0.4544 rather than 1.0 because within candidate count > 1 the outcome is a DETERMINISTIC index tie-break, not a probabilistic draw: decide() maximises (posterior, -index), so among tied survivors it deterministically returns the LOWEST index. The residual variance is therefore Bernoulli sampling noise around a deterministic rule, not unexplained variation.

second_unifying_finding.label: REPLICATED
second_unifying_finding.statement: q == 1/candidates EXACTLY, to floating-point precision (max deviation 5.55e-17), in every arm and every stratum. The degenerate confidence metric is a property of the uniform posterior over the explaining set, not an artefact of a particular prior. It was mis-measured in Run 2 (D9), not absent.

boundary_conditions: B1: The entire three-run trajectory reduces to ONE variable. Candidate-set size determines success; success determines q; q determines 1/candidates. Relevance, information content, and hypothesis-elimination accounting are all redescriptions of this single quantity in this substrate.

B2: Every operation is a hard mask, so the posterior is uniform on the surviving explaining set by construction. No experiment in this substrate can produce a graded posterior, and therefore none can distinguish 'how much the belief moved' from 'how many hypotheses survived'. These are not merely correlated here; they are the same object.

B3: Because decide() uses a deterministic lowest-index tie-break, 'success' is not a stochastic guess. Any construct that varies only WHICH hypotheses survive will produce apparent 'relevance effects' that are pure index artefacts.

B4: To discriminate relevance as a causal variable, the substrate must be changed: soft/graded likelihoods (so the posterior can be non-uniform on the explaining set) and a randomised or genuinely uncertain decision rule.
what_run3_established: Candidate-set size, not relevance, is the single operative variable (F3.1, R3E3).
The relevance effect Run 2 reported is real descriptively but non-causal.
The distractor-consistency competing explanation is falsified (R3E4).
what_run3_failed_to_establish: Whether relevance is causal in a substrate with graded posteriors -- untestable here (B2).
Whether the deterministic lowest-index tie-break is an artefact of this implementation or a deeper property -- it is an implementation fact of decide() and should not be generalised.
Anything about real human communication or real feedback.
unresolved_discriminations: U1 (RESOLVED): is relevance causal? NO, within this substrate.
U2 (UNRESOLVED): does candidate-set size remain the single variable once the posterior can be non-uniform on the explaining set? Requires soft likelihoods -- a substrate change.

U3 (UNRESOLVED): the deterministic index tie-break means success is not a sample from the posterior. Whether a randomised decision rule would restore relevance effects is untested and testable ONLY with a substrate change.
U4 (UNRESOLVED, carried from Run 1): the lexical-repair crossover failure remains unexplained and was never revisited in Runs 2 or 3.

meta_question_for_next_stage.question: Does the collapse to a single variable (candidate-set size) survive a substrate in which the posterior can be non-uniform over the explaining set, or is that collapse an artefact of hard masking plus a deterministic tie-break?
meta_question_for_next_stage.derivation: Run 3 established B1-B4: every operation is a mask, the posterior is uniform on the explaining set by construction, and decide() returns the lowest-index survivor. Under those three properties, candidate count necessarily determines success, and relevance has nowhere to act. The collapse is therefore NOT yet shown to be a property of the phenomenon -- only of this substrate. U2 and U3 both require the same minimal change, and no experiment within the current substrate can address either.

quality_tests.novelty_within_trajectory: PASS. No prior run asked whether its own substrate's degeneracy was the cause of its results. Runs 1-3 each found a confound (degenerate prior, relevance/candidate confound, marginal-vs-conditional) and repaired it WITHIN the substrate. This asks whether the substrate itself is the confound.
quality_tests.evidence_derivation: PASS. Forced by B1-B4 and U2/U3, which are direct consequences of the Run 3 measurements.
quality_tests.operationalizability: PARTIAL. Requires a substrate change (soft likelihoods + randomised decision rule), so it is NOT executable in the current environment. This is stated as a boundary, not glossed.
quality_tests.falsifiability: PASS. If a soft-likelihood substrate with a randomised tie-break STILL shows candidate count as the sole predictor, the collapse is a property of the phenomenon and is confirmed. If relevance or graded posterior mass regains predictive power, the collapse is an artefact and Run 3's account is overturned.
quality_tests.non_closure: PASS. Genuinely open and not answerable here.
